rejected.title: Trigonometry on the unit circle
card: The unit circle has radius 1 and its centre at the origin. Take a point on it, at an angle \(\theta\) measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.
The x-coordinate of the point is \(\cos \theta\). The y-coordinate is \(\sin \theta\). So the point is \((\cos \theta, \sin \theta)\).
This works for any angle up to 360\(^{\circ}\). In the second quadrant, x is negative, so \(\cos \theta\) is negative. Below the x-axis, y is negative, so \(\sin \theta\) is negative.
Example: at 90\(^{\circ}\) the point is \((0, 1)\), so \(\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\) and \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 1\). At 180\(^{\circ}\) the point is \((-1, 0)\), so \(\cos 180^{\circ} = -1\).

2.alt: The unit circle with a point P at 60 degrees from the positive x-axis. A radius of length 1 joins the centre to P. P has x-coordinate cos theta and y-coordinate sin theta, marked by dashed lines to the axes.

rejected.remember: On the unit circle, the point at angle \(\theta\) is \((\cos \theta, \sin \theta)\), so the signs follow the quadrant.

a.q: A point on the unit circle at angle \(\theta\) has coordinates \((0.6, 0.8)\). What is \(\sin \theta\)?
a.why: The y-coordinate of the point is \(\sin \theta\), so \(\sin \theta = 0.8\). The value 0.6 is the x-coordinate, which is \(\cos \theta\), so it is the tempting swap.

b.q: A point on the unit circle is at \(270^{\circ}\) from the positive x-axis. It is at \((0, -1)\). What are \(\cos 270^{\circ}\) and \(\sin 270^{\circ}\)?
b.why: The x-coordinate is 0, so \(\cos 270^{\circ} = 0\). The y-coordinate is \(-1\), so \(\sin 270^{\circ} = -1\). Swapping the coordinates gives the tempting second option.
b.clue: Read the x-coordinate first, then the y-coordinate.

version.title: Trigonometry on the unit circle
card: The unit circle has radius 1 and its centre at the origin. Measure an angle \(\theta\) anticlockwise from the positive x-axis to a point \(P\) on the circle.
The x-coordinate of \(P\) is \(\cos \theta\) and its y-coordinate is \(\sin \theta\), so \(P\) is the point \((\cos \theta, \sin \theta)\).
This defines sine and cosine for any angle from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\). Left of the y-axis, \(\cos \theta\) is negative. Below the x-axis, \(\sin \theta\) is negative.

2.alt: The unit circle, centred at the origin with radius 1. A point P on the circle in the first quadrant has dashed guides to the axes: its x-coordinate is \(\cos \theta\) and its y-coordinate is \(\sin \theta\).

version.remember: Cosine is across and sine is up: they are the coordinates of the point on the unit circle.

a.q: A point on the unit circle at angle \(\theta\) is \((-0.6, 0.8)\). What is \(\cos \theta\)?
a.why: The x-coordinate is \(\cos \theta\), so \(\cos \theta = -0.6\). The value \(0.8\) is the y-coordinate, which is \(\sin \theta\).

b.q: \(P\) is the point on the unit circle at \(180^{\circ}\). What are \(\cos 180^{\circ}\) and \(\sin 180^{\circ}\)?
b.why: At \(180^{\circ}\), \(P\) has turned halfway round to \((-1, 0)\). Its x-coordinate gives \(\cos 180^{\circ} = -1\), and its y-coordinate gives \(\sin 180^{\circ} = 0\). Swapping them reads the coordinates the wrong way round.
b.clue: Where is the point half a turn from \((1, 0)\)?
